Stratification

strat-uh-fih-KAY-shun · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Stratification means the arrangement of people or things into distinct, ranked layers or levels.

Beneath the polite dinner conversation lay a rigid stratification, in which the seating itself announced who stood above whom.

Worked Example

On the naval vessel, the crew was divided into sharply ranked layers, with senior officers berthed on the upper decks, petty officers just below them, and enlisted sailors packed into the cramped lower quarters near the hull.

Stratification means arrangement into DISTINCT, RANKED LAYERS stacked one above another by status or level. It is not just any grouping or sorting (you can separate people into equal categories that have no top and no bottom); stratification specifically requires LAYERS THAT SIT ABOVE AND BELOW ONE ANOTHER in a fixed order of rank. The crew split across higher and lower decks strictly by rank is the definition of stratification.

How Stratification Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

hierarchy

hierarchy: A system of ranked levels of authority; stratification emphasizes the layered separation of a whole population into those levels, not just a top-down chain of command.

ranking

ranking: Ranking orders individual items along a single scale from top to bottom; stratification gathers them into distinct layers or bands, each holding many members at a similar level.

layering

layering: Layering captures the stacked, level-upon-level structure, but it can be purely physical or neutral, whereas stratification implies the layers carry differing rank or status.

Antonyms

egalitarianism

egalitarianism: The principle that all people are equal and belong to no ranked layer; it directly opposes stratification's division of a population into higher and lower levels.

uniformity

uniformity: A state of being the same throughout, with no distinct layers or levels to rank — where stratification stacks differences, uniformity erases them.

How Strong Is It? — mixed → grouped → stratification

mixed vs. stratification

mixed vs. stratification: A mixed crowd has no order at all, while stratification locks everyone into distinct layers ranked one above another.

grouped vs. stratification

grouped vs. stratification: Grouped items sit in separate but equal categories; stratification goes further by stacking those groups into higher and lower ranks.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — strati-

Root — strati-: something spread or laid down; a layer (Latin stratum, from sternere, 'to spread out' — the i is the linking vowel that joins it to the suffix)

Suffix — -fication

Suffix — -fication: the act or process of making (from Latin facere, 'to make, do')

Put it together

Put it together: Strati- (a layer — Latin stratum, 'something spread or laid down,' from sternere, 'to spread out,' plus its linking vowel) + -fication (the act of making — from Latin facere) = layer-making: taking a whole population, society, or material and laying it down in distinct sheets, one stacked above another — which is why the word always implies ranked levels, never just separate side-by-side groups.

Use the root in a new word: substrate

Use the root in a new word: substrate: Chemists prepared a clean glass substrate first, since every thin film they deposited afterward had to bond to that base layer underneath.

Word Choice

Formal / academic

Stratification is the precise term for arrangement into ranked layers, especially in sociology, geology, and ecology. In everyday speech, say 'the class system,' 'levels,' or 'pecking order,' but stratification is the exact word when you want to emphasize a whole system divided into distinct, ranked layers.
